title: The Gig Economy: Freedom or Insecurity?

passage.title: The Gig Economy: Freedom or Insecurity?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Ten years ago, few people had heard the term gig economy. Today, millions of workers earn money by delivering food, driving passengers or completing small online tasks through apps and platforms. Supporters present it as a revolution in flexibility; critics call it a return to the insecurity of nineteenth-century casual labour. As someone who has studied the sector for several years, I believe both descriptions contain some truth, but that the critics currently have the stronger case.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The attractions are real. Gig workers choose when and how long they work, which suits students, parents with young children and people who need a second income. Entry is easy: there are no interviews, and an account can be opened in a day. Surveys in several countries show that many workers value this independence highly, and a significant proportion say they would not accept a regular job even if it were offered.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Yet flexibility often turns out to be limited. Workers are paid per task, and the platform decides how many tasks are available and at what price. Many report that to earn a reasonable wage, they must be online at times of high demand, such as evenings and weekends, which leaves them little real choice. When calculated per hour, including time spent waiting for orders and the cost of fuel, a number of studies found earnings below the legal minimum wage.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The greater problem is security. Because gig workers are classed as self-employed, they receive no sick pay, holiday pay or pension contributions. A worker who is injured on a delivery has to bear the cost of lost income. In 2021, a court in the UK ruled that a group of drivers should be treated as workers entitled to a minimum wage and paid holidays, and other countries are considering similar rules. The companies argue that this would destroy the flexibility that workers want.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: I do not think it would. Several platforms that have accepted regulation continue to operate, and their workers report the same freedom to choose their hours. The solution is not to ban gig work but to give those who do it basic protections. A society should not allow the cost of risk to be passed entirely to the people least able to bear it.

items.prompt: What do supporters of the gig economy claim?
Why is it easy to start gig work?

options.text: Workers receive free training before starting
There are no interviews and an account opens in a day

items.explanation: The text says: "there are no interviews".

items.prompt: What does the writer say about flexibility in practice?

options.text: Workers often need to be online at busy times
Workers can choose any hours without penalty
Workers can set their own prices

evidence.quote: must be online at times of high demand

items.explanation: The text says: "must be online at times of high demand".

items.prompt: What did a number of studies find about hourly earnings?

options.text: They were the same as in regular jobs
They were sometimes below the minimum wage

evidence.quote: earnings below the legal minimum wage

items.explanation: The text says: "earnings below the legal minimum wage".

items.prompt: What did the 2021 UK court decide?

options.text: Some drivers should be treated as workers with rights
Platforms must close in the United Kingdom
All gig workers are legally self-employed

evidence.quote: should be treated as workers entitled to a minimum wage

items.explanation: The text says: "should be treated as workers entitled to a minimum wage".
